food-webs-s2.title: Sea otters and kelp forests
food-webs-s2.passage: Along parts of the North Pacific coast, sea otters were hunted almost to extinction for their fur in the 1700s and 1800s. Where otters disappeared, sea urchins, which graze on kelp, became very numerous, and many kelp forests were reduced to bare rock called "urchin barrens." Where otters were protected and returned, urchins became scarce and kelp grew back, along with the many fish that shelter in kelp. Ecologists use this as an example of how one predator can shape a whole community, though they note that storms, water temperature and urchin disease also affect kelp.
food-webs-s2.source: Invented passage for practice, summarizing widely reported ecology of North Pacific kelp forests.

items.q: How is a food web different from a food chain?
options: A food web shows the producers and leaves out consumers.
A food chain includes more species than a food web.
A food web shows the flow of water, not of energy.

why.correct: A food chain is one line of who eats whom; a food web joins many chains, since most organisms eat and are eaten by several species.
options: Right: a web is many interconnected chains.
A web contains many chains, so it has more species.

items.q: Earthworms and millipedes eat dead leaves and break them into smaller pieces. What are they?

why.correct: Detritivores eat detritus, dead organic matter, and break it up, which speeds up decomposition by fungi and bacteria.
options: They do not hunt living prey.
They eat dead leaves, not live animals.

items.q: Why are food webs with many links usually more stable than simple ones when one species declines?
options: Complex webs lack predators, so prey are safe.
Complex webs do not need producers at the base.
Simple webs hold more energy at each level.

why.correct: With several food sources, consumers can shift to another, so the decline of one species does not collapse the rest.
options: Right: other food sources soften the change.
Web complexity does not add energy.

items.q: What would happen to nutrients in an ecosystem if all decomposers and detritivores disappeared?
options: Nutrients would stay locked in dead matter.
Producers would grow faster with fewer competitors.
Nothing, since decomposers are outside the food web.
Energy would cycle back to the producers instead.

why.correct: Decomposers release the nutrients in dead matter back to the soil and water. Without them dead matter piles up and producers starve for nutrients.
options: Right: the nutrient cycle would stall.
Producers would lack nutrients and grow less.
Decomposers are a key part of every web.
Energy does not cycle; it leaves as heat.

items.q: A predator is removed and its prey, a plant-eater, multiplies. Which change is most likely next?

why.correct: More plant-eaters eat more plants, so plants decline: an effect that cascades two levels down from the predator.
options: Right: more grazing means fewer plants.
More plant-eaters means more plants eaten, not more plants.
With no predator, the plant-eater grows at first.

items.q: In a pond, a disease kills most of the algae. Build the chain for what happens to the fish that eat zooplankton (which eat algae).

why.correct: Less algae → less food for zooplankton → zooplankton decrease → fish that eat them have less food and decrease.

specific.frame: Fewer algae means ___ food for zooplankton, so zooplankton ___, and the fish that eat them ___.

why.1: Algae are the zooplankton’s food; fewer algae means less food.
Fewer zooplankton means less food for the fish.

specific.model: Fewer algae means less food for zooplankton, so zooplankton decrease, which leads to the fish that eat them having less food and decreasing.

items.q: In a food chain, what does each arrow represent?
options: Energy moving from food to eater
Water moving down through the soil
A predator chasing after its prey

why.correct: Arrows show energy (and the matter in food) moving from food to consumer.
options: Right: energy and matter move along the arrow.
The arrow points from prey to predator, the direction of energy, not of the chase.
Competition is not shown by feeding arrows.

items.q: Grass → rabbit → fox. If a drought kills much of the grass, which change comes first?
options: Rabbits have less food and decline.

why.correct: The rabbits eat the grass directly, so they feel the loss first; the foxes feel it later, as rabbits decline.
options: Right: the grass-eaters lose food first.
Foxes have fewer rabbits to eat, so they would not increase.

items.q: In the food web, which organisms eat the mouse?

why.correct: Arrows from the mouse point to the snake, the fox and the hawk.
options: Frogs eat grasshoppers; grasshoppers eat grass.
Rabbits eat plants, so they do not eat mice.

items.q: If a disease wiped out the frogs, which population would most likely increase first?

why.correct: Frogs eat grasshoppers; without frogs, fewer grasshoppers are eaten.
options: Snakes lose a food source, so they would not increase.
Shrubs are not eaten by frogs or grasshoppers in this web.

items.q: Why would losing the frogs probably not wipe out the snakes?

why.correct: The web shows an arrow from mouse to snake, so snakes have another food source.

items.q: At which trophic levels does the hawk feed in this web?

why.correct: Rabbits and mice are primary consumers, so eating them puts the hawk at level 3; snakes are secondary consumers, so eating them puts it at level 4.

items.q: What is the main claim of the passage?
options: Otters protect kelp by eating urchins.
Sea urchins are the main predators of sea otters.
Storms are the one real cause of urchin barrens.
Kelp forests grow best where there are no fish.

why.correct: Where otters returned, urchins declined and kelp regrew; the passage presents otters as shaping the community.
options: Otters eat urchins, not the reverse.
The passage lists storms as one factor among others.
Fish shelter in kelp; nothing says kelp grows best without them.

items.q: Which evidence in the passage best supports the claim?
options: Otters were hunted for their fur.
Many fish shelter in the kelp.
Sea urchins graze on the kelp.

why.correct: The before-and-after contrast (otters gone, kelp lost; otters back, kelp regrows) is the evidence that links otters to kelp.
options: Right: the comparison links otters to kelp.
That explains why otters disappeared, not their effect.
That is a result of kelp, not evidence of the otter effect.
That is part of the mechanism, not evidence that otters matter.

items.q: Why does the passage mention storms, water temperature and urchin disease?
options: To prove that otters cause storms.
To argue that otters harm the kelp.
To show urchins do not eat the kelp.

why.correct: It notes other influences so the reader does not credit otters with every change.
options: Right: a caution about other causes.
The passage says otters help kelp.
The passage says urchins graze on kelp.
